title: AI Pipelines Specialty Exam
description: 20 questions drawn from a pool of 36, focused on concepts and workflow patterns rather than specific pipeline implementations. Pass mark is 80%. Open-book — browse any page, hover glossary terms, or ask the AI assistant. Your answers are saved as you go. Explanations appear after submission.

questions.prompt: What does tokenisation do to a prompt before the model can process it?
options: Translates the prompt into the model's native language
Splits the text into smaller units the model can map to vectors
Encrypts the prompt for transit to the server
Filters out profanity and personal information
questions.explanation: Tokenisation splits the input into manageable units — whole words, syllables, or punctuation — that the embedding step then maps to vectors. It is a standardisation step before any real understanding takes place.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - AI Specialty: AI-PDI Pipelines — Tokenisation

questions.prompt: Why do similar concepts cluster together in an embedding space?
options: Because the model alphabetises the vocabulary
Because vectors are assigned in dictionary order
Because training learns to place related meanings at nearby coordinates
Because each word has a fixed numeric ID and similar IDs are adjacent
questions.explanation: Embeddings are learned representations: the training objective pushes semantically related tokens to similar coordinates, so 'dog' lands closer to 'cat' than to 'bicycle'.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - AI Specialty: AI-PDI Pipelines — Embeddings

questions.prompt: Inside the transformer, which mechanism lets the model link words that are far apart in a sentence?
options: Sliding window
Attention
Recurrent feedback
Beam search
questions.explanation: The attention mechanism lets tokens influence each other across long distances — the core innovation behind the transformer architecture.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - AI Specialty: AI-PDI Pipelines — Transformers & Attention

questions.prompt: Generation in an LLM happens one token at a time. What guides each next-token choice?
options: A random number generator with a fixed seed
Whichever token appears most often in the training data
A probability distribution over candidate tokens, sampled or argmaxed
The token the user typed, shifted by one position
questions.explanation: The model outputs a probability distribution over the vocabulary at each step; sampling strategies (greedy, top-k, top-p, temperature) pick the next token from that distribution.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - AI Specialty: AI-PDI Pipelines — Generation

questions.scenario: A team can rank documents either by literal keyword overlap or by embedding-space distance, and wants to understand the trade-off.
questions.prompt: What is the practical difference between keyword search and vector (semantic) search?
options: Keyword search is always faster than vector search
Keyword matches surface lexical overlap; vector search ranks by meaning similarity in embedding space
Vector search only works on text in English
Keyword search returns documents; vector search returns single sentences
questions.explanation: Keyword search rewards literal token overlap. Vector search compares embedding-space distance, so semantically related results surface even when no keywords match.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - AI Specialty: AI-PDI Pipelines — Semantic Search

questions.scenario: A pipeline scores two passages for relatedness by comparing their embeddings with cosine similarity.
questions.prompt: What does a cosine similarity value close to 1.0 indicate?
options: The vectors point in nearly the same direction — the texts are semantically very similar
The vectors are perpendicular — the texts are unrelated
The two texts are identical character-for-character
The model has zero confidence in the result
questions.explanation: Cosine similarity measures the angle between two vectors. Values near 1.0 mean they point in almost the same direction, which for embeddings means high semantic similarity.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - AI Specialty: AI-PDI Pipelines — Semantic Search

questions.prompt: The transformer architecture is composed of which two main blocks?
options: Encoder and decoder
Tokenizer and detokenizer
Trainer and inferer
Embedder and quantizer
questions.explanation: Transformers stack an encoder (processes the input sequence) and a decoder (generates the output sequence). Both use attention; GPT-style models are decoder-only.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - AI Specialty: AI-PDI Pipelines — Transformers & Attention

questions.prompt: Why is positional encoding added to token embeddings before the transformer?
options: It compresses the embedding to half its size
Attention is order-agnostic, so positional encoding injects 'where in the sequence' information back in
It is required to authenticate the request
Without it the model would always output the same token
questions.explanation: Self-attention treats tokens as a bag and has no notion of order. Positional encodings restore sequence position so 'dog bites man' and 'man bites dog' stay distinguishable.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - AI Specialty: AI-PDI Pipelines — Transformers & Attention

questions.scenario: Two prompts in a deduplication check come back with a cosine similarity of 0.05 in embedding space.
questions.prompt: What does that value suggest about the two prompts?
options: They are nearly identical
They are unrelated — the vectors are close to perpendicular in meaning space
One prompt is much longer than the other
Both prompts triggered the same model response
questions.explanation: Cosine values near 0 mean the vectors are roughly perpendicular — semantically unrelated. Near 1 means similar; near -1 means opposite (rare in normalised embedding spaces).
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - AI Specialty: AI-PDI Pipelines — Semantic Search

questions.prompt: Why is an LLM's context window a practical limit on what a single call can handle?
options: The model can only output a fixed number of tokens
Each token in the context consumes capacity; once the window is full, older tokens drop out and the model loses access to them
Context windows are decorative and don't actually limit anything
It is a licensing restriction
questions.explanation: The context window caps how many tokens (system prompt + history + retrieved context + question) the model can attend to at once. Large workflows split work into stages or use RAG to stay under the cap.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - AI Specialty: AI-PDI Pipelines — Context Window

questions.scenario: A docs-grounded pipeline must return the same answer for the same prompt on every run so results are reproducible.
questions.prompt: What does setting the temperature sampling parameter to 0 produce?
options: A completely random response each time
Deterministic, repeatable output — the model always picks the highest-probability token
An empty response
Only single-character responses
questions.explanation: Temperature scales the probability distribution. At 0, sampling collapses to greedy decoding, so the same prompt yields the same output every time. Higher values flatten the distribution and increase diversity.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - AI Specialty: AI-PDI Pipelines — Temperature & Sampling

questions.prompt: Why can different tokenizer encodings (e.g. cl100k_base vs p50k_base) produce different token counts for the same text?
options: Newer encodings always produce fewer tokens
They use different vocabulary sizes and merge rules learned during training, so the same word may split into more or fewer sub-tokens
Token counts are random by design
They include the model's IP address as a token
questions.explanation: Each tokenizer was trained with its own BPE merges and vocabulary. The same string can decompose into different sub-token sequences depending on which encoding processes it.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - AI Specialty: AI-PDI Pipelines — Tokenisation

questions.scenario: A PDI pipeline must send a product photo to a multimodal LLM whose API accepts only a JSON body.
questions.prompt: What is the standard way to carry that binary image inside the JSON request?
options: Embed the raw bytes directly in the JSON body
Encode the binary as a text-safe string (typically Base64) so it survives JSON serialisation and HTTP transit
Convert the image to ASCII art first
Send the image separately by FTP
questions.explanation: JSON cannot carry raw binary cleanly. Base64 encodes any bytes as ASCII characters that fit inside a string field — the same pattern used by every multimodal LLM API.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - AI Specialty: GenAI — Base64 Encoding

questions.scenario: A pipeline scrapes web pages, but each page carries navigation, scripts, and footers around the article body before it reaches the LLM.
questions.prompt: What does extracting just the relevant elements before sending the HTML achieve?
options: Reduces token spend by dropping navigation, scripts, and footers
Sharpens the model's focus on the meaningful content
Helps stay within the model's context-window limit
Makes HTML readable by the model, which otherwise cannot parse tags at all
questions.explanation: Pre-extraction (XPath, CSS selectors, readability heuristics) keeps only the meaningful content — lowering cost, improving answer quality, and leaving more room in the context window. The model can read raw HTML; the point is to trim noise, not to make it parseable.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - AI Specialty: GenAI — HTML Extraction (XPath / CSS)

questions.prompt: How does RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) improve an LLM's answers?
options: By re-training the model on every new question
By retrieving relevant context from a knowledge source and feeding it into the prompt before generation
By caching previous answers and returning them verbatim
By compressing the prompt with gzip before sending
questions.explanation: RAG keeps the base model frozen but supplies relevant context at inference time — embedding both the question and the corpus, retrieving the top-k similar passages, and adding them to the prompt.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - AI Specialty: GenAI — RAG

questions.prompt: In a chat interaction, what do the 'system', 'user', and 'assistant' roles do?
options: Identify which person on your team typed each message
Mark each message's origin so the model knows what to follow as instructions, what to answer, and what is prior conversation
Control which network port the message uses
Nothing — the model ignores them
questions.explanation: Roles structure the conversation. The system role sets persona and rules, user provides input, and assistant carries previous model responses so multi-turn context is preserved.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - AI Specialty: GenAI — Roles & Prompt Context

questions.scenario: An ingestion workflow must accept PDF, DOCX, XLSX, and even password-protected PDFs, then feed their text to an LLM.
questions.prompt: What is the typical architectural choice for handling that format variety?
options: Hand-write a parser for each format
Use a content-extraction library (e.g. Tika) that handles many formats and returns plain text, so the rest of the pipeline only deals with strings
Reject everything that is not already plain text
Train a custom LLM to read every format
questions.explanation: A general-purpose extraction layer such as Tika absorbs format variety. Downstream, every step sees only text, which keeps the LLM-facing logic simple and reusable.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - AI Specialty: GenAI — Document Ingestion (Tika)

questions.prompt: In a GenAI-augmented ETL pipeline, where does PDI typically sit in the architecture?
options: Inside the LLM as a sampling strategy
As the orchestration layer that prepares context, calls the LLM, parses the response, and routes the result to downstream sinks
As a replacement for the model entirely
Only as a logging consumer at the end
questions.explanation: PDI is the conductor: it assembles structured and unstructured inputs, hands them to the model with the right prompt, parses the response, and writes typed results back to databases, files, or APIs.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - AI Specialty: GenAI — PDI as Orchestration Layer

questions.scenario: A pipeline runs the same classification prompt across thousands of data rows, substituting only the row's text into a fixed structure.
questions.prompt: Why is prompt templating useful in this case?
options: It eliminates the need for a model entirely
It keeps the instructions consistent across every row while only the input data varies, making outputs comparable and reproducible
It compresses the prompt to half its size
It is required by HTTP
questions.explanation: A stable instruction skeleton with variable slots means every row gets the same framing — easier to evaluate, debug, and iterate on the prompt without breaking comparability.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - AI Specialty: GenAI — Prompt Templating

questions.scenario: A workshop runs its model through Ollama on the VM rather than calling a hosted cloud API.
questions.prompt: What is the main advantage of running the LLM locally?
options: Local models are always smarter than cloud ones
Sensitive data stays inside your network, there is no per-call cost, and latency is predictable — at the price of managing the infrastructure yourself
Local models support more programming languages
Cloud APIs do not support JSON
questions.explanation: Local hosting via Ollama trades operational overhead for privacy, cost predictability, and offline capability. For sensitive data or high-volume inference, that trade often makes sense.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - AI Specialty: LLM Integration — Local Inference with Ollama

questions.scenario: An LLM returns its answer as a JSON string, but the next steps need to join and aggregate on individual fields.
questions.prompt: Why is a parsing step almost always needed before downstream consumers can use the response?
options: To decrypt the response
Because the model emits text — even JSON arrives as a string and its typed fields must be extracted before joining, aggregating, or writing it
To translate the response
To rate-limit the next call
questions.explanation: Models emit strings; ETL consumers want columns. A parse step (JSON Input, regex, split fields) converts the raw response into typed records the rest of the transformation can manipulate.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - AI Specialty: LLM Integration — Parsing the Response (JSON Input)

questions.prompt: Named Entity Recognition (NER) is most useful when you need to:
options: Count the words in a document
Pull typed entities — people, organisations, places, dates — out of free-form text so downstream steps can filter, mask, or join on them
Encrypt the document
Render the document to HTML
questions.explanation: NER turns narrative into rows. Once entities are tagged you can route, redact PII, build search indexes, or join the text to structured master data.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - AI Specialty: LLM Integration — Named Entity Recognition

questions.prompt: What characterises a 'multi-staged' LLM workflow?
options: It uses multiple programming languages
Each LLM call has a single focused purpose, and the output of one stage becomes the input to the next — e.g. classify, then enrich, then summarise
It runs the same prompt many times in parallel
It requires multiple physical servers
questions.explanation: Decomposing a complex task into focused stages keeps each prompt tight, makes errors easier to localise, and lets you mix model sizes (cheap classifier feeding an expensive synthesiser).
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - AI Specialty: LLM Integration — Multi-staged Pipelines

questions.scenario: A pipeline's throughput is dominated by LLM inference latency, and the team wants to raise records-per-minute without changing the model.
questions.prompt: Which design responses are effective ways to raise throughput?
options: Batch multiple records into one call when the model supports it
Fan rows out in parallel so several calls are in flight at once
Add more 'Select values' steps and rename fields
Convert the transformation to a job
questions.explanation: Batching amortises per-call overhead; parallelism uses idle wait time. Together they are the standard knobs for raising throughput on LLM-dominated pipelines. Renaming fields or converting to a job does nothing for inference latency.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - AI Specialty: LLM Integration — Throughput & Performance

questions.prompt: When is text summarisation an appropriate pipeline step?
options: When you want to compress JSON
When long-form documents need to be turned into shorter, structured summaries that human reviewers or constrained downstream context windows can consume
When you are translating to another language
When you are counting tokens
questions.explanation: Summarisation collapses verbose input into a focused output — useful when the downstream consumer has tight context limits, or when humans need to skim large volumes quickly.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - AI Specialty: LLM Integration — Text Summarisation

questions.prompt: Why is data enrichment via an LLM a useful step in a modern ETL pipeline?
options: It cleans up character encoding
It adds structured fields the source lacked — classifying a free-text description into a category, or detecting language — without hand-coded rules
It compresses the dataset
It is required for GDPR
questions.explanation: Enrichment fills gaps the source cannot. Classification, language detection, intent labelling, and country inference are all derivable from free text by a model that already understands meaning.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - AI Specialty: LLM Integration — Data Enrichment

questions.scenario: A sentiment-analysis pipeline returns both a label and a confidence score for each customer review.
questions.prompt: What is the typical workflow pattern for using that confidence score?
options: Discard the confidence and trust every label equally
Use the score to gate downstream decisions — high-confidence rows flow through automatically, low-confidence rows route to human review
Multiply the score by the row count
Treat any non-zero score as positive sentiment
questions.explanation: Confidence-thresholded routing is the standard pattern: trust the model when it is certain, escalate when it is not. This scales automation without sacrificing quality on edge cases.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - AI Specialty: LLM Integration — Sentiment Analysis & Confidence Thresholds

questions.scenario: A pipeline must extract fields from support tickets and clinical notes where the same fact is reworded, reordered, or paraphrased across records.
questions.prompt: Why does an LLM-based extractor outperform regex on these natural-language inputs?
options: Regex is slower
Regex matches literal patterns; the model handles reworded, reordered, and paraphrased information without an explosion of rules
Regex does not support Unicode
Regex requires Python
questions.explanation: Natural language varies — synonyms, reorderings, abbreviations, typos. Each variation needs a new regex; one LLM handles them all by reading for meaning.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - AI Specialty: LangExtract — Why LLM Extraction over Regex

questions.scenario: A LangExtract pipeline tags some tickets with an urgency label of 'CRITICAL' before the rows reach a reviewer or router.
questions.prompt: Why is making that label visually prominent in the output useful?
options: It is purely cosmetic
Downstream consumers — humans or routers — can act on the most important rows immediately without scanning the whole list
It speeds up the LLM
It is required by accessibility law
questions.explanation: Extracted priority is only useful if it changes behaviour. Visual emphasis (colour, badge, sort key) ensures urgent rows get attention first, whether the consumer is a person or an automated routing rule.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - AI Specialty: LangExtract — Surfacing Urgency

questions.prompt: Why wrap an LLM extraction component in a REST service rather than embedding it in every pipeline?
options: REST is the only way to call Python from PDI
A service centralises the schema, model choice, and prompt — so every pipeline gets the same extraction logic and upgrades happen in one place
REST is faster than function calls
It encrypts traffic automatically
questions.explanation: Centralising the extractor as a service means model swaps, prompt tweaks, and schema upgrades roll out once. Every consumer just POSTs text and a schema; the service does the rest.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - AI Specialty: LangExtract — REST Service Pattern

questions.scenario: A developer needs to pull dates, parties, and monetary amounts out of free-form contract clauses.
questions.prompt: What is the LangExtract workflow for this?
options: Train a custom BERT model from scratch on the contracts
Send the clause text along with a schema that names the target fields and types; the service returns those fields populated
Convert every contract to PDF and parse the layout
Write a regex per field and chain them
questions.explanation: LangExtract takes text plus a schema and asks the LLM to populate the fields. The same pattern works for tickets, clinical notes, and contracts — only the schema changes.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - AI Specialty: LangExtract — Schema-driven Extraction

questions.prompt: What is the architectural difference between an 'LLM-enriched ETL step' and a genuine AI agent?
options: Agents are written in Python; LLM steps are written in Java
An LLM step is a pure function (input to response in one pass); an agent runs a loop, using intermediate output to decide what tool to call next before producing a final answer
Agents always cost more than steps
Agents can only run on Linux
questions.explanation: A step calls the model once. An agent reasons over partial output, fetches more data, calls the model again, and converges on an answer — it is a loop, not a function.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - AI Specialty: Agent-as-a-Service — Agent vs LLM Step

questions.scenario: An architect is deciding whether a new requirement should be built as PDI steps or as an agent.
questions.prompt: What is a useful heuristic for that decision?
options: Whether the team prefers Python or Java
Whether the task decomposes into deterministic steps (regex, lookups, joins); if cross-text reasoning is required, that is agent territory
Whether the data exceeds 1 GB
Whether the use case involves images
questions.explanation: If PDI can do it by adding more steps, do it in PDI — it is deterministic and observable. If the work needs the model to reason over previous output to choose its next move, that is an agent.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - AI Specialty: Agent-as-a-Service — When to Use an Agent

questions.scenario: An agent must fetch related fault history mid-reasoning before it can classify the current entry, and the lookup target is unknown until the first LLM call completes.
questions.prompt: How does the agent obtain that external information?
options: A hard-coded SQL string inside the prompt
Tools — named capabilities exposed to the agent that it can choose to invoke, with the response fed back into its next reasoning step
Random sampling
Renaming its model
questions.explanation: Tool use is the agent pattern. The agent decides 'I need X', calls the tool, reads the result, and uses it to refine its answer. PDI orchestrates the pipeline; the agent decides what to fetch.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - AI Specialty: Agent-as-a-Service — Tool Calling

questions.prompt: Beyond 'the response looks right', what should you check to validate that an agent is working correctly?
options: Inspect the reasoning trace and logs to confirm the agent chose reasonable tools
Confirm the final structured output matches the expected schema
Check that the pipeline runs in under a second
Compare the prompt to the response character-for-character
questions.explanation: Agents are loops, so you validate the loop: did it pick reasonable tools and did intermediate results look sensible, and did the final structured output match the schema? Raw speed and character-for-character comparison say nothing about whether the agent reasoned correctly.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - AI Specialty: Agent-as-a-Service — Validating an Agent

questions.prompt: Why is exposing an agent as a service (rather than embedding it inside a PDI step) the typical deployment pattern?
options: PDI does not support Python
Agents need persistent state, tools, and a Python ecosystem; a service keeps the agent reusable across pipelines and isolates its runtime from PDI's
Services run faster than steps
License restrictions
questions.explanation: Wrapping the agent as a service means PDI stays the orchestrator and many pipelines can call the same agent. Updates, model swaps, and tool additions roll out once at the service.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - AI Specialty: Agent-as-a-Service — Deployment Pattern
